contentBody: **A student asks an AI tool: "Which quarter had the highest revenue?" The AI answers, then the student asks: "Now break that quarter down by region — which region drove most of that growth?" What technique is this student practising?**
option.1: A guided exploratory follow-up (EDA-style prompt chain)
option.2: Zero-shot prompting with no context at all
option.3: Asking the AI to hallucinate a plausible-sounding region
answerExplanation: Asking a first question, then a sharper follow-up that reacts to the answer, is exactly the guided exploratory pattern this lesson teaches — look at the data from more than one angle before concluding anything.

contentBody: **A comparison shows Region X converting at 60% (built from 500 customers) and Region Y converting at 65% (built from only 12 customers). Why should Region Y's number be treated with more caution?**
option.1: It should not — a higher percentage is always more trustworthy
option.2: Region Y's number is impossible to calculate at all
option.3: Region Y's percentage is built on a much smaller sample size and could swing wildly by chance
option.4: Percentages built on fewer customers are always exactly accurate
answerExplanation: A percentage built on very few data points is far less reliable than one built on a large sample — a small sample size is one of the clearest warning signs that a "finding" might just be noise.

contentBody: **Four variables are tested against a conversion outcome: Variable A spans 15%–95% across its groups; Variables B, C, and D each span less than 8 points across their groups. Which is the most reasonable next step?**
option.1: Treat all four variables as equally important and act on all of them at once
option.2: Investigate Variable A further; treat B, C, and D as likely flat and set them aside for now
option.3: Ignore Variable A because a wide spread always means the data is broken
option.4: Discard all four variables because any spread under 100 points is meaningless
answerExplanation: A wide, consistent spread (like Variable A's) is the signal worth chasing. Variables with only a few points of spread are close to flat and are a valid, useful "nothing here" finding, not a reason to manufacture a story.
